case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act authorizes U.S. courts to hear “trafficking” suits against Cuban state-owned entities without requiring plaintiffs to satisfy an exception to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. §§ 6081–6085, and the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 (especially the baseline grant of immunity and the requirement of a statutory exception for jurisdiction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Title III was enacted specifically to create an effective U.S. damages remedy for victims of Cuba’s confiscations and to reach the state-owned entities that received or exploit expropriated property; reading Title III to require plaintiffs to separately fit within a FSIA exception would largely defeat Congress’s design because most Helms‑Burton trafficking claims would be jurisdictionally barred. Exxon (supported by the United States and business amici) contends that Title III supplies the necessary authorization to sue Cuban agencies/instrumentalities (i.e., it functions as a carve-out or satisfies FSIA’s requirement that immunity yields where Congress clearly provides otherwise), so courts should not superimpose FSIA-exception pleading as an additional gatekeeping requirement that Congress did not write into Title III.
case_analysis.respondent_position: CIMEX and the other Cuban respondents argue that the FSIA is the comprehensive, exclusive framework for suing foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, so a plaintiff must always establish a FSIA exception unless Congress unmistakably and explicitly overrides immunity. Respondents contend Title III does not clearly abrogate FSIA immunity for Cuba or its instrumentalities, and therefore cannot be read to dispense with FSIA’s jurisdictional prerequisites. They further emphasize separation-of-powers and international-law/reciprocity concerns—warning that implying an immunity override would contradict FSIA’s structure, invite diplomatic friction, and risk encouraging foreign courts to disregard sovereign immunity protections for the United States and U.S. instrumentalities.

John Roberts.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point is that Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially undercut if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity, implying an intended override. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the FSIA is a comprehensive jurisdiction-and-immunity framework: §1604 supplies the baseline immunity and §1330(a) makes an enumerated exception a prerequisite to the court’s power, and we require unmistakable clarity before treating a later statute as displacing that structure. Title III reads as a liability rule and contains no clear abrogation of immunity, no amendment adding an FSIA exception, and no jurisdictional grant that bypasses §1330; reading silence as repeal would convert a targeted remedial statute into an all-purpose jurisdictional hook—precisely what our FSIA precedents reject. Given the foreign-relations consequences, the narrower, text-faithful holding is that Title III does not itself waive or abrogate FSIA immunity, leaving plaintiffs to proceed only if an existing FSIA exception and §1608 service are satisfied.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially weakened if Cuban instrumentalities retain FSIA immunity, but that functional concern cannot supply a jurisdictional waiver Congress did not clearly enact. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the FSIA makes the presence of an enumerated exception the exclusive, jurisdictional “term of consent,” and Title III contains no unmistakable textual statement displacing §1604 or §1330(a)’s gatekeeping. Reading Title III’s silence as an implied abrogation would improperly enlarge the waiver and invite courts to create an extra-statutory exception in a foreign-relations-sensitive area Congress addressed comprehensively in the FSIA. Title III can still operate as a liability rule when a plaintiff satisfies an existing FSIA exception and complies with §1608 service requirements; absent that, the courts lack power to proceed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is functional: Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially diminished if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FSIA is an interlocking and exclusive jurisdictional scheme—§1604 supplies the baseline immunity and §1330 ties both subject-matter and personal jurisdiction to the statute’s enumerated exceptions plus proper service under §1608. Title III reads as a liability-creating provision, not an unmistakably clear abrogation of sovereign immunity or an amendment adding a new FSIA exception, and we have no warrant to infer a waiver from silence in an area with acute foreign-relations implications. Title III can still operate where an existing FSIA exception applies; treating it as an implied override would effectively create an extra-statutory exception that the FSIA’s structure forbids.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Title III’s Cuba-specific “trafficking” cause of action would be substantially weakened if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity, implying Congress must have meant to reach them. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, FSIA establishes a baseline presumption of immunity and an exception-by-exception jurisdictional gate, and we require unmistakable clarity before treating a later statute as displacing that framework. Title III reads like a liability rule—defining who may be liable for trafficking—without supplying the jurisdictional consent or an explicit amendment to §1604 or §1330, and inferring an override from purpose would effectively create a new FSIA exception “without more.” Title III can still operate coherently where plaintiffs plead and prove an existing FSIA exception (and comply with §1608), so preserving the FSIA’s structure best respects Congress’s calibrated scheme in this foreign-relations-sensitive domain.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is functional: Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” in confiscated property would be significantly weakened if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke FSIA immunity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, FSIA is an exclusive, exception-by-exception jurisdictional framework, and we do not treat a later statute’s silence as an implied repeal of §1604 or a new, extra-textual immunity exception. Title III reads as a liability rule, not an immunity override or jurisdictional grant, and it can still do work where an existing FSIA exception supplies the necessary consent to suit. Given Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak clearly when it displaces immunity, Title III’s absence of unmistakable abrogation language forecloses petitioner’s theory.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is functional: Title III’s remedial scheme would be meaningfully narrowed if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity, so Congress must have intended an implicit override. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Congress in 1976 supplied a comprehensive, rule-like baseline of immunity in §1604 and made the enumerated FSIA exceptions the exclusive path to jurisdiction; a later statute creating liability does not, by silence, amend that jurisdictional gatekeeping. Accepting an implied abrogation here would invite precisely the ad hoc, purpose-driven immunity determinations the FSIA displaced, and nothing in Title III contains the unmistakably clear statement we have demanded when Congress intends to alter foreign-sovereign immunity. Title III can still do work where an existing FSIA exception applies, so we need not—and should not—manufacture a new exception from inference.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Title III is Cuba-specific and broadly authorizes suit against any “person” who “traffics,” which would often include Cuban state-owned entities—so, the argument goes, Congress must have meant to reach them notwithstanding the FSIA. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FSIA is a comprehensive, interlocking jurisdiction-and-immunity scheme for civil actions against foreign states and their instrumentalities, and we have required unmistakable clarity before reading a later statute to abrogate §1604 immunity or bypass §1330’s exception-based gatekeeping. Title III reads as a liability rule and does not speak in the jurisdictional/waiver terms Congress typically uses when it intends to displace sovereign immunity; treating silence plus remedial purpose as an implied repeal would effectively create a new FSIA exception by judicial inference. Title III can still operate where an existing FSIA exception applies and where plaintiffs comply with §1608 service—policy consequences are for Congress or the Executive, not atextual expansion by the courts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest petitioner-side point is that Title III’s remedial design—targeting trafficking in confiscated Cuban property—would be substantially frustrated if Cuban instrumentalities retain FSIA immunity. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito stress, the FSIA is an exclusive, interlocking jurisdiction-and-immunity scheme, and we require an unmistakably clear statement before treating a later statute as abrogating §1604 or bypassing §1330(a)’s exception-based gatekeeping. Title III reads as a merits-conferring cause of action, not a jurisdictional override; remedial purpose and broad “person” language cannot supply the missing waiver, especially in a foreign-relations-sensitive setting where Congress legislated comprehensively. Title III can still operate where an existing FSIA exception applies, so recognizing immunity here respects both statutes’ text and structure without creating an extra-textual exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is functional: Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” in confiscated property seems designed to reach Cuban state-linked entities, and requiring an FSIA exception could narrow that remedy. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, remedial breadth cannot substitute for the “unmistakably clear” statutory consent needed to overcome the FSIA’s exception-by-exception, jurisdictional gatekeeping in §§ 1604 and 1330(a). Title III reads like a merits/liability provision (defining wrongful “trafficking”), not a jurisdictional waiver, and treating it as an implied immunity override would improperly collapse the threshold waiver inquiry into the substantive elements of the claim. Because Title III can still operate where an existing FSIA exception supplies jurisdiction (and §1608 service is satisfied), I do not see a textual or structural basis to infer a new, extra-statutory exception.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA establishes a baseline presumption of immunity that deprives courts of subject-matter jurisdiction unless a specifically enumerated exception applies, and we construe departures from that framework narrowly to avoid turning statutory causes of action into all-purpose jurisdictional hooks. Title III creates a civil liability scheme for "trafficking," but it does not speak with the unmistakable clarity needed to abrogate a foreign state’s immunity or dispense with the FSIA’s jurisdictional gatekeeping, particularly as to Cuban state-owned entities that qualify as agencies or instrumentalities. Reading Title III to authorize suit without a FSIA exception would be a radical departure from the FSIA’s structure and would predictably heighten foreign-relations friction and reciprocal exposure for the United States absent clear congressional direction. Plaintiffs therefore must still identify a valid FSIA exception before a federal court may hear Title III claims against Cuban state-owned entities.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Foreign sovereign immunity is jurisdictional, so a federal court lacks power to proceed unless Congress has clearly waived immunity and the plaintiff strictly satisfies the waiver’s conditions. The FSIA supplies the exclusive basis for jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, and it requires a statutory exception to immunity as a term of the sovereign’s consent to suit. Title III creates a cause of action, but it does not unmistakably abrogate FSIA immunity or dispense with FSIA’s jurisdictional prerequisites for Cuban state-owned entities, and courts may not enlarge any waiver beyond the statute’s text—especially given the foreign-relations consequences of implied immunity overrides. Because plaintiffs here cannot proceed absent a valid FSIA exception, the suits must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the exclusive, comprehensive framework for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities in our courts, and it links both subject-matter jurisdiction (§ 1330(a)) and personal jurisdiction (§ 1330(b)) to satisfaction of a statutory immunity exception plus proper service under § 1608. Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act creates a cause of action against those who “traffic” in confiscated property, but it does not contain the sort of unmistakably clear statement that displaces the FSIA’s baseline grant of immunity in § 1604 or dispenses with the Act’s exception-based prerequisites. Reading Title III to authorize suit against Cuban state-owned entities without any showing of a § 1605–1607 exception would effectively graft a broad, implied immunity override onto a tightly interlocking statutory scheme—an extra-textual move inconsistent with Congress’s choice to make immunity turn on the FSIA’s enumerated exceptions. Because plaintiffs therefore must proceed, if at all, within an applicable FSIA exception and comply with § 1608 service, the judgment should favor respondents.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FSIA establishes a baseline presumption of foreign sovereign immunity, and U.S. courts may exercise jurisdiction over a foreign state or its agencies/instrumentalities only if the plaintiff fits the case within a statutory exception. Nothing in Title III of the Helms–Burton Act unmistakably displaces that comprehensive framework or supplies, on its own, a jurisdictional grant overcoming immunity; reading Title III to bypass the FSIA would effectively dilute the Act’s element-by-element exception structure and invite courts to proceed “without more” than Congress required in the FSIA. On these facts, Exxon therefore must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception (such as the commercial-activity or expropriation exception) as a jurisdictional prerequisite, rather than relying on Title III as an implied immunity override. That approach respects the FSIA’s codification of the restrictive theory of immunity and avoids reflexive, policy-driven departures from Congress’s chosen scheme.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA sets the baseline rule: a foreign state and its agencies/instrumentalities are immune unless a plaintiff identifies a specified statutory exception, and our cases describe it as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction in civil actions against foreign sovereigns. Title III creates a cause of action against any “person” who traffics in confiscated property and may contemplate that some defendants will be state-owned entities, but it nowhere contains an unmistakable statement displacing FSIA immunity or supplying a new immunity exception; reading Title III to bypass the FSIA would therefore require inferring an abrogation Congress did not clearly make. And a structural, comparative reading cuts the same way: when Congress intends to overcome foreign sovereign immunity, it typically does so expressly and with targeted language, so the omission of any FSIA override in Title III looks deliberate rather than accidental. Because Title III can operate fully as a liability provision once a plaintiff satisfies an existing FSIA exception, I would not treat it as silently repealing or circumventing the FSIA’s jurisdictional prerequisites.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule: foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities "shall be immune" from suit unless a plaintiff can bring the case within one of Congress’s enumerated exceptions, and this comprehensive scheme is the exclusive route to civil jurisdiction over such defendants. Title III of Helms‑Burton creates a cause of action for "trafficking," but it nowhere clearly and unmistakably displaces the FSIA’s immunity grant or adds a new FSIA exception applicable to Cuban state-owned entities, so we should read Title III as operating within (not outside) the FSIA’s framework. Accepting petitioner’s theory would convert a later statute’s silence about immunity into an implied abrogation, contrary to the FSIA’s rule-like structure Congress adopted in 1976 to replace ad hoc, nonuniform practice. Because respondents are Cuban state-owned entities that qualify as a "foreign state" or "instrumentality" under §§ 1603–1604, and petitioner has not identified an applicable FSIA exception on these facts, jurisdiction is barred.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: To begin with, the FSIA’s text and structure establish a comprehensive, exclusive scheme governing civil actions against foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities, with jurisdiction in federal court running through § 1330 only when a specified FSIA exception applies. Title III of Helms-Burton creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not contain the kind of clear, express statutory text displacing the FSIA’s immunity-and-jurisdiction framework or adding an independent jurisdictional grant that bypasses § 1330’s exception requirement. Petitioner's policy and foreign-relations arguments about Congress’s remedial goals cannot substitute for the statutory work Congress would have had to do to override the FSIA as written; if broader abrogation is desired, that is for Congress (or the Executive via suggestions of immunity) to address. Consistent with the Court’s repeated statements and practice treating the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states in civil cases, Title III must operate within the FSIA’s exceptions rather than silently supersede them.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule: foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities are immune from suit in U.S. courts unless a statutory exception applies, and this Court has repeatedly described the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state. Applying a text-and-structure-first approach, Title III’s creation of a trafficking cause of action and its references to liability for Cuban entities do not unmistakably displace FSIA’s jurisdictional gatekeeping or identify any FSIA exception that fits; reading an implied carveout would rest on a free-floating structural inference rather than a clear congressional directive. Because Congress built the FSIA as a comprehensive framework and did not expressly override its immunity rule in Helms–Burton, plaintiffs must still plead and prove an FSIA exception for Cuban state-owned entities. Any broader reading would expand judicial power in a foreign-relations-sensitive area absent the clarity this Court demands when Congress is said to strip sovereign immunity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FSIA immunity is a jurisdictional bar that a court must resolve at the threshold, and Congress must speak with unmistakable clarity to permit suits against a foreign state or its agencies/instrumentalities. Reading Title III’s creation of a “trafficking” cause of action to dispense with FSIA’s exception-by-exception jurisdictional gate would improperly convert a remedial statute into an implied immunity override, even though FSIA’s structure makes it the “sole basis” for jurisdiction absent an express carve-out. Title III contains no clear textual waiver/abrogation of FSIA immunity for Cuban state-owned entities, and the fact that requiring an FSIA exception may narrow Title III’s practical reach does not authorize courts to rewrite the immunity prerequisite that Congress otherwise imposed through FSIA. Because plaintiffs here seek jurisdiction over Cuban instrumentalities without identifying a specific FSIA exception that applies, the suits must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act authorizes suits against Cuban agencies and instrumentalities for “trafficking” in expropriated property without requiring plaintiffs to plead and prove an applicable exception to sovereign immunity under the FSIA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082 (and related provisions), in interaction with the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 (especially the presumption of immunity and statutory exceptions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Title III creates a federal cause of action intended to reach Cuban state-controlled entities that possess or commercially exploit confiscated U.S. property and that Congress meant this remedy to be available against Cuban agencies/instrumentalities without the additional hurdle of fitting the claim into an FSIA exception. Exxon and supporting amici emphasize that requiring FSIA-exception proof would frustrate Helms‑Burton’s remedial and deterrent design (compensation and accountability for Castro-era expropriations), because the most plausible FSIA pathways (e.g., expropriation/commercial activity exceptions) can be difficult to satisfy on their elements (nexus requirements, characterization of conduct, and jurisdictional gatekeeping). The United States as amicus supports petitioner, stressing U.S. foreign-policy interests in enabling Title III suits to promote accountability and compensation for U.S. victims and urging an interpretation under which Title III operates as a congressional authorization that is not defeated by the FSIA’s default immunity framework.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Corporación CIMEX and other respondents argue that the FSIA supplies the exclusive basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, so a Title III claim may proceed only if an FSIA statutory exception applies. They contend Helms‑Burton does not clearly and expressly displace the FSIA’s immunity regime; absent unmistakable congressional intent, courts must apply FSIA first and dismiss claims barred by sovereign immunity. Respondents and supporting international-law/sovereign-immunity scholars warn that reading Title III to bypass FSIA would conflict with the FSIA’s structure (immunity as the default, exceptions narrowly construed), create foreign-relations friction, and would be out of step with international practice reflected in comparative materials (including doctrines akin to avoiding indirect impleading of a foreign sovereign and respecting sovereign immunity when adjudication would require passing on the legality of another state’s public acts).
key_precedents: No specific U.S. Supreme Court merits precedents are expressly identified in the provided excerpts; the briefing centers on statutory interpretation of Helms‑Burton Title III in relation to the FSIA.

Comparative/foreign authorities referenced in the international-law materials include: Cerbuco v. Family Brewers, Dutch Court of Appeals of ’s‑Hertogenbosch (23 July 2024), ECLI:NL:GHSHE:2024:2380; Central Santa Lucia LC v. Meliá Hotels International SA, Jdo Primera Instancia No. 24 Palma de Mallorca, Auto 00036/2023 (27 Jan. 2023) (Spain); and a South African Supreme Court of Appeal discussion of indirect impleading (case name not included in the excerpt).

John Roberts.reasoning: I remain with Respondent. The petitioner’s strongest point is the anti-nullification argument—that Title III’s broad “person” and “trafficking” language would be blunted if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke immunity—but, as Justice Kagan notes, we do not infer an immunity displacement from general authorization to sue, especially where Congress has enacted a comprehensive jurisdictional scheme in the FSIA. The FSIA makes immunity the baseline and an enumerated exception the prerequisite for jurisdiction; Title III creates a cause of action but does not speak in the unmistakable terms (immunity, jurisdiction, or amendment to § 1605) required to override that framework. Treating Title III as a freestanding “hook” would risk converting a targeted remedial statute into an implied, uncodified exception that collapses the FSIA’s gatekeeping inquiry into the merits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is the anti-nullification argument—that Title III’s broad “person” definition and trafficking cause of action would be substantially blunted if Cuban instrumentalities remain immune. But as Justice Kagan explains, that is a purpose-based inference, and it cannot supply the unmistakable textual clarity needed to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive, jurisdictional scheme making immunity the baseline and enumerated exceptions the sole gateway. I agree with the Chief Justice that reading Title III as a freestanding jurisdictional hook would manufacture an uncodified “Helms–Burton exception,” contrary to the FSIA’s strict conditions on the sovereign’s consent to be sued. Under strict construction, Title III may create liability, but plaintiffs must still plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception as a prerequisite to jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention is that Title III would be largely toothless against Cuban instrumentalities unless we treat it as an implicit immunity override. But the FSIA establishes a bright-line presumption of immunity in § 1604, and § 1330 links jurisdiction to the statute’s enumerated exceptions; that integrated design is not displaced by purpose-driven inferences from a separate cause of action. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Title III does not speak in the language Congress ordinarily uses to abrogate immunity or amend the FSIA, and we should not manufacture an uncodified “Helms–Burton exception” by implication. Title III may supply the substantive claim, but a plaintiff still must satisfy an FSIA exception before a federal court may exercise jurisdiction over a foreign state or instrumentality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention is the anti-nullification point: Title III’s broad definition of covered “persons” and creation of civil liability would be significantly weakened if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan underscore, the FSIA is the exclusive, jurisdictional gateway for suits against foreign states and their instrumentalities, and displacement requires an unmistakably clear statement—something Title III lacks because it does not speak in immunity or jurisdictional terms, nor does it amend § 1605’s calibrated exceptions. Treating Title III as an implied immunity override would be a radical, atextual departure from the restrictive theory Congress codified, collapsing the FSIA’s threshold gatekeeping into the merits and inviting generalized, non-elemental pleading rather than the specificity the FSIA demands. Accordingly, plaintiffs must still plead facts satisfying an enumerated FSIA exception before Title III’s cause of action can proceed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains the anti-nullification argument: Title III’s broad definition of liable “persons” would be substantially undercut if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke FSIA immunity. But as the Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the FSIA is a comprehensive, exclusive gateway—§ 1604 sets the baseline and Congress displaces it only with unmistakable clarity, typically by amending the FSIA or expressly authorizing enforcement suits that immunity would otherwise defeat. Title III reads as a substantive cause of action that operates only once amenability to suit is established; it does not speak in immunity or jurisdictional terms, and treating it as an implied “Helms-Burton exception” would collapse the FSIA’s threshold inquiry into merits liability, contrary to § 1606’s separation principle. The right rule is therefore: Title III supplies a claim, but plaintiffs must still plead and prove an enumerated FSIA exception (such as commercial activity or expropriation) to hale a foreign instrumentality into court.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s anti-nullification point—that Title III’s broad authorization to sue any “person” who “traffics” would be largely blunted if Cuban instrumentalities may claim immunity—has real force as a policy matter, but it cannot supply the clear textual hook needed to displace the FSIA’s baseline rule in § 1604. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FSIA is the comprehensive, jurisdictional gateway: courts may not manufacture an implied “Helms–Burton exception” from liability language that never speaks in immunity or jurisdictional terms. Accepting petitioner’s theory would invite precisely the atextual “grafting” the FSIA was designed to prevent, collapsing the threshold immunity inquiry into the merits and bypassing Congress’s carefully enumerated § 1605 exceptions. The more faithful reading is that Title III supplies a cause of action that operates only once a plaintiff independently satisfies an FSIA exception (e.g., commercial activity or expropriation).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point is the anti-nullification argument—that Title III’s broad liability for any “person” who “traffics” would be largely frustrated if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke FSIA immunity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FSIA is a comprehensive, carefully calibrated jurisdiction-and-immunity scheme in which immunity is the baseline and only enumerated exceptions open the courthouse door; Title III creates a cause of action but nowhere speaks in unmistakable jurisdictional or immunity-displacing terms. Reading Title III as an implied override would effectively manufacture a new FSIA exception by implication, contrary to the FSIA’s text, structure, and our repeated characterization of the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states and instrumentalities. Any policy concerns about Title III’s practical reach are for Congress and the Executive to address through explicit amendments, not for us to supply by inference.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is the anti-nullification argument: that Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who traffics would be significantly undermined if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke FSIA immunity. But as the Chief Justice explains, the FSIA is the exclusive, comprehensive jurisdictional gateway, and we require an unmistakably clear statement before treating another statute’s liability language as displacing that scheme. Justice Kagan’s point is decisive for me: reading Title III to do immunity work by implication would collapse the FSIA’s threshold immunity inquiry into the merits and effectively create an uncodified “Helms–Burton exception,” contrary to the FSIA’s enumerated-exceptions design. Title III is therefore necessary, but not sufficient—plaintiffs must still plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception to establish jurisdiction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is the anti-nullification argument: Title III’s cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be significantly undermined if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke FSIA immunity. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the FSIA is Congress’s comprehensive, jurisdictional gateway, and displacement of that scheme requires an unmistakably clear statement in statutory text—Title III does not speak in immunity, jurisdiction, or FSIA-amendment terms. Treating Title III’s general liability language as an implied immunity override would effectively manufacture an uncodified FSIA exception, collapsing the threshold immunity inquiry into the merits in a way §1604’s structure resists. Title III can supply the cause of action, but plaintiffs must still plead and prove an enumerated FSIA exception with statute-tethered, nonconclusory allegations.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule: foreign states and their agencies and instrumentalities are presumptively immune, and a federal court has jurisdiction only if the plaintiff brings the claim within a specifically enumerated FSIA exception. Reading Title III’s creation of a “trafficking” cause of action to dispense with that jurisdictional prerequisite would convert a targeted Cuba-specific remedy into a broad immunity “hook,” collapsing the restrictive-theory distinction by exposing quintessentially sovereign public acts (the underlying expropriations and their consequences) to suit without Congress having spoken in the FSIA’s terms. Nothing in Title III clearly and expressly displaces the FSIA’s comprehensive immunity framework; at most it supplies a substantive cause of action that may be pursued only where an FSIA exception (such as commercial activity or expropriation, if satisfied) independently establishes jurisdiction. That reading fits the FSIA’s text–context–history structure and avoids a radical departure from the Act’s carefully limited exceptions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA "provides the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction" over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, so a federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction unless the plaintiff can bring the case within an enumerated FSIA exception. Title III of Helms-Burton creates a cause of action for "trafficking," but it does not contain a clear, express waiver of foreign sovereign immunity or an unmistakable displacement of the FSIA’s carefully delineated immunity and exception framework; under strict construction, I would not infer such a waiver from remedial purpose or general authorization to sue. Because Congress attached immunity and exception requirements as the terms on which foreign states may be haled into U.S. courts, those conditions define the scope of any permissible suit here, and plaintiffs must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception before proceeding. Allowing Title III claims to bypass the FSIA would expand liability and jurisdiction beyond what Congress clearly authorized in text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA establishes a bright-line rule of presumptive immunity for foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities, and it provides the exclusive, comprehensive framework for jurisdiction unless an enumerated FSIA exception applies. Title III of Helms–Burton creates a cause of action against those who “traffic” in expropriated property, but it does not expressly amend the FSIA or supply a clear, administrable immunity override; reading it to bypass FSIA would create an atextual immunity exception and reintroduce the very uncertainty Congress eliminated in the FSIA. Under § 1330(a)–(b), jurisdiction over a foreign state-linked defendant normally follows only when an FSIA immunity exception is satisfied, and nothing in Title III’s text displaces that linkage for Cuban instrumentalities. Because plaintiffs therefore must plead and prove a valid FSIA exception to proceed, the suit cannot go forward on Title III alone.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole and exclusive” basis for subject-matter jurisdiction over suits against a foreign state or its agencies and instrumentalities, so plaintiffs must plead facts bringing their claim within a statutory exception before a U.S. court may hale a Cuban instrumentality into court. Title III creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but nothing in its plain text unmistakably displaces the FSIA’s baseline presumption of immunity or purports to create a freestanding jurisdictional grant overriding § 1330(a) and the FSIA’s carefully calibrated exceptions. Reading Title III to bypass the FSIA would be a radical expansion inconsistent with the restrictive theory of sovereign immunity and Congress’s choice to require threshold, element-by-element satisfaction of an exception as the jurisdictional gatekeeper. Whatever the moral force of the expropriation allegations, the threshold question is jurisdiction, and absent a clearly applicable FSIA exception (pleaded with the specificity the statute demands), the suit must be dismissed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule: Cuban agencies and instrumentalities are immune from suit unless a specified FSIA exception applies, and that immunity is jurisdictional. Title III creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it nowhere clearly states that Cuban sovereign immunity is displaced, nor does it expressly authorize suit against a “foreign state” in a way that would necessarily be nullified unless immunity were removed; absent such a clear statement, I would not infer an implied override of the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Reading Title III to bypass the FSIA would collapse the immunity inquiry into the merits (who is liable for trafficking) and would contradict the FSIA’s structural premise that amenability to suit must be established first through an enumerated exception. Plaintiffs therefore must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception (such as the expropriation or commercial-activity exceptions) before a Title III claim may proceed against a Cuban instrumentality.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule that foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities are immune from suit in our courts, and it makes jurisdiction turn on whether the plaintiff can fit within one of the statute’s enumerated exceptions. Nothing in Title III’s text unmistakably displaces that framework or creates a free‑standing “Helms‑Burton exception” to immunity, and I would not graft such an atextual carveout onto the FSIA’s unambiguous terms. Reading the statutes together, Title III may create a cause of action, but the FSIA still governs whether a court may exercise jurisdiction over a Cuban instrumentality, so plaintiffs must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception (such as the commercial-activity or expropriation exception) to proceed. That approach respects Congress’s comprehensive immunity scheme and preserves the judiciary’s duty to apply enacted law rather than expanding jurisdiction based on policy aims or executive-branch preferences.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA’s text and structure make immunity the default rule in any “civil action” against a foreign state or its agencies and instrumentalities, and they make an FSIA exception a prerequisite to subject-matter jurisdiction under § 1330(a). Title III of Helms–Burton creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not clearly and expressly displace the FSIA’s comprehensive, carefully calibrated jurisdiction-and-immunity scheme; absent such a clear statement, courts must apply the FSIA “as written” and require plaintiffs to plead and prove an applicable exception. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would effectively create a new, uncodified immunity exception by implication, contrary to the FSIA’s design and this Court’s repeated characterization of the FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over foreign states in U.S. courts. Policy and foreign-relations arguments about Helms–Burton’s deterrent purpose cannot justify rewriting the statutory boundary Congress drew in the FSIA; any adjustment is for Congress and the President.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the baseline rule and (as this Court has repeatedly said) the exclusive basis for jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, so a plaintiff must plead and prove a statutory FSIA exception to overcome immunity. Title III’s creation of a federal cause of action for “trafficking” is, at most, a necessary step toward relief; it does not by itself displace the FSIA’s separate, interlocking immunity gatekeeping unless Congress clearly says so. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would imply a carveout from a comprehensive, centralized immunity scheme—precisely the sort of implied departure from sovereign-immunity doctrine and statutory structure that our cases resist absent unmistakable textual grounding. Because Title III lacks a clear statement abrogating foreign sovereign immunity or amending the FSIA framework, the suit cannot proceed without an applicable FSIA exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The FSIA establishes the baseline rule that foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities are immune from suit unless a statutory exception applies, and any displacement of that regime must be "unmistakably clear" in Congress’s text and structure. While Title III creates a cause of action for "trafficking" and defines covered "persons" broadly enough to reach foreign instrumentalities, it does not, by its own explicit terms, speak to jurisdiction, immunity, or otherwise clearly indicate that Congress meant to override the FSIA’s immunity framework rather than operate within it. Given the FSIA’s design to cabin judicial power through specifically delineated exceptions, I would not infer an implied abrogation from Title III’s general liability language and definitional cross-references; plaintiffs must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception to proceed. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would expand liability beyond what Congress made clear on the face of the statute, contrary to the narrow, text-tethered approach required for sovereign-immunity questions.
